name: KISS, YAGNI and Premature Abstraction
intent: Build the simplest thing that does today's job, and add flexibility when a real change asks for it, except where a mistake is very expensive to fix later, such as a public API or a stored data format.
scenario: A team has to export a report as CSV. Someone suggests an exporter interface, a registry, a config file and a factory, because JSON, XML and PDF are bound to come. Twelve months later one of those formats has been asked for, in a shape the interface did not expect, and the other two were never written. Meanwhile the team shipped a plain file format with no version field, and adding one field now means breaking every program that reads old files.
problem: KISS (keep it simple) and YAGNI (you aren't gonna need it) are usually heard as: do not plan, do not generalise. The sharper reading is about cost and evidence. Every option you build for a future nobody has asked for has a price now, in code to read, test and carry, and a price later, when the real change arrives in a shape you did not guess and the speculative structure is in the way. But the rule is not a ban on thinking ahead: some decisions are cheap to make later and some are not, and the second kind deserves a little planning up front.

howItWorks.title: Price what you build for a guess
howItWorks.text: Speculative generality is code that exists for a requirement nobody has. A plug-in interface with one plug-in, a factory that returns one class, a config flag with one value. It does no harm when you run it, which is why it survives, but each piece is something the next reader must trace through: in the sample, one report goes through 7 calls instead of 1. You pay that cost every day whether or not the guess ever comes true.

howItWorks.title: Count what a wrong guess costs
howItWorks.text: The guess pays off only if the future arrives in the shape you built for. When it arrives differently, you have two problems: the structure you must change, and the structure you must work around. In the simulation, speculation breaks even with plain code only when about 9 of 10 guesses are right. Few people guess that well, which is the practical content of YAGNI: it is a statement about your hit rate, not about taste.

howItWorks.title: Keep the code easy to change instead of ready for change
howItWorks.text: The alternative to prediction is cheap change. Small functions, clear names, tests that tell you when you broke something. Then the day the second format is asked for, you add it with the real example in front of you, and the abstraction is shaped by two true cases instead of one imagined. This is also why the rule of three in the DRY concept exists: abstract from evidence.

howItWorks.title: Plan ahead where change is expensive
howItWorks.text: Some decisions cost little to change later: an internal function, a private class. Others cost a great deal once other people depend on them: a public API, a wire protocol, a database schema, a file format that is already written to disk. For those, a little foresight is cheap insurance: a version field, room to add fields without breaking readers, a rule that unknown versions are rejected loudly. In the sample, an old reader silently misreads a new unversioned record, while a versioned one says it does not know the version.

howItWorks.title: Tell speculation from foresight
howItWorks.text: A useful test: if the guess is wrong, how bad is it? Speculative code you can delete in an afternoon is cheap to be wrong about. A public contract you cannot take back is not. Plan the second kind, keep the first plain, and do not mistake a wish for a requirement. KISS and YAGNI, like DRY, are heuristics that pull against other heuristics, and the judgement is in knowing which cost you are facing.

pros: Less code to read, test and keep working, so every real change is cheaper to make
Abstractions are shaped by real examples, so they fit when they finally appear
A small design is easy to delete, which makes a wrong turn cheap
Planning only the hard-to-reverse parts spends effort where it is worth the most
cons: Some later changes will cost more than if you had planned for them, and you will feel that cost
Deciding what is hard to reverse takes judgement and knowledge of who depends on the code
'Keep it simple' is easy to stretch into never refactoring, which makes the simple version complicated by accretion
A team that distrusts planning can ship a public format with no room to grow
whenToUse: Internal code whose callers you control and can change in one commit
A first version of a feature, where you do not yet know what will vary
Anywhere you are tempted to add a parameter, interface or config switch with exactly one value
whenNotToUse: Public APIs, wire formats, database schemas and stored files, where a late change breaks other people's code: version them and leave room to grow from the start
Security, data loss and legal rules, where 'we will add it when needed' means after the incident
As a reason to skip tests, naming or structure: simple does not mean careless
pitfalls: Building the plug-in system for the second, third and fourth implementation, when only the first exists, and finding the interface fits none of them
Reading YAGNI as 'never think ahead' and shipping a file format or API with no version field, then needing a breaking change for the first new field
Calling something simple because it is short: a dense one-liner that nobody can read is not simple, it is only small
Confusing simple with easy: copying the nearest example is easy, but the design that results may be far from simple
Leaving unused options in place because deleting feels wasteful; an option nobody uses still has to be understood, tested and kept compatible
Treating a config flag as free flexibility: every flag doubles the states the code can be in, and each combination is a place for a bug
Using 'we might need it' as the whole argument: ask what it would cost to add it later, and what it costs to carry it now

roles.label: Change request
roles.description: A new requirement as it really arrives, not as it was guessed.

roles.label: Plain code
roles.description: The simplest implementation of today's job.

roles.label: Speculative layers
roles.description: Interfaces, registries and config built for futures nobody asked for.

roles.label: Public contract
roles.description: A format or API that other people's code depends on.

roles.label: Outside readers
roles.description: Programs and files you cannot change in one commit.

quiz.question: A teammate wants to add an interface, a factory and a config key for a second export format that nobody has asked for. What does YAGNI say?
options: Build it now, because adding structure later always costs more than adding it today.
Wait for the real second format, and then shape the abstraction from two true cases.
Build the factory but leave the config key out, so the work is split in two.
Write the interface only, because an interface has no behaviour and so no cost.
quiz.explanation: Structure built for a guess is carried and read every day, and it must still fit the real request when it comes. Waiting lets the second case shape the abstraction. An interface with one implementation is not free: someone has to read and maintain it.

quiz.question: Your service writes files that other teams' programs will read for years. Which decision deserves planning now, despite YAGNI?
options: A plug-in system for exporters, in case a new team asks for one.
Which internal helper function should hold the parsing code.
A version field and a rule that readers reject versions they do not know.
The name of a private variable inside the writer, to avoid later renaming.
quiz.explanation: A stored format is expensive to change once files and readers exist, so a version field is cheap insurance. A plug-in system and internal names can be changed in one commit whenever needed.

quiz.question: In a model where a speculative design costs 6 extra up front, saves 1 per correct guess and costs 2 more per wrong guess, why does it usually lose to plain code?
options: Plain code is always faster to write, whatever the future turns out to bring.
Speculative designs cannot be tested, so their guesses are never checked at all.
Interfaces slow the program down by an amount that grows with each new format.
Wrong guesses cost more than plain code, so it pays only if nearly all are right.
quiz.explanation: The build cost is paid at once, the savings arrive only on correct guesses, and a wrong guess costs more than plain code would have. Break-even needs a very high hit rate, which is rare for guesses about the future.
